articles.title: Node.js Polling Cost Explained for Device Presence (More Viewers, Event Fan-Out)
articles.excerpt: A media operations dashboard has one unforgiving requirement: a device shown as online should actually be online. Once several people watch the same fleet, repeated polling spends reads to rediscover…
articles.body: A media operations dashboard has one unforgiving requirement: a device shown as online should actually be online. Once several people watch the same fleet, repeated polling spends reads to rediscover mostly unchanged state, while each viewer sees a different-age answer. I would calculate presence once on the server and push each change to connected dashboards. Polling still belongs in recovery and low-attention screens. Short answer: pushing wins above a handful of viewers when viewers x polls per minute exceeds the real change rate plus the overhead of open connections. The threshold is not a universal head count. Presence accuracy, payload size, query cost, and event frequency decide it. Why does pushing beat polling above a handful of viewers?

articles.body: If a column addition isn't reflected in the drizzle snapshot, the next drizzle-kit generate re-emits an ADD COLUMN without IF NOT EXISTS . Starting with the conclusion For a column addition with no new table involved, don't rerun drizzle-kit generate — hand-edit the snapshot ( drizzle/meta/*.json ) directly to reflect the column definition. Leave it unreflected and the next generate will judge that column "not yet existing," re-emitting an ADD COLUMN with no IF NOT EXISTS . Applying that ALTER to an environment where the column already exists (via a hand-written migration) fails.

articles.title: Scoping a Keyright license to an environment: migrating from one key everywhere to a signed staging/production boundary
articles.excerpt: Watch a single license file long enough and it ends up everywhere. You issue one key for the product, drop it into the production deployment, and within a sprint it has been copied into the staging en…
articles.body: Watch a single license file long enough and it ends up everywhere. You issue one key for the product, drop it into the production deployment, and within a sprint it has been copied into the staging environment so the pre-prod smoke tests pass, pasted into a developer's appsettings.Development.json , and baked into a CI secret so integration tests can run. Now four environments present the same signed key to your Keyright instance, and three facts you would like to have are gone: you cannot tell from a validation which environment it came from, a staging key that leaks is a production key, and the day you want to expire the staging key early you discover it is the production key. This post is a migration guide.

articles.title: Twenty-four searches, twelve answers: what our own catalog search measures
articles.excerpt: A marketplace usually answers "can a buyer find what they need?" with a supply we have N endpoints. That number says nothing about the query an The measurement is boring and reproducible, which is the…
articles.body: A marketplace usually answers "can a buyer find what they need?" with a supply number: we have N endpoints . That number says nothing about the query an agent actually types. We took 24 real search terms from a public 30-day demand preview, ran each one verbatim against our own catalog, and counted what came back. Twelve answered. Every one of the five zeros was the same missing capability. The measurement is boring and reproducible, which is the point: one GET per term, a hit count, and a reading of why. No sampling, no survey. 1. How our search actually matches Our catalog search is a literal token AND. A query is split into tokens, and a row matches only if every token appears in its description (or name). There is no stemming, no synonym table, and no relevance ranking to hide behind.

articles.title: Decompiling checked arithmetic: add.ovf, conv.ovf, and rebuilding the checked block
articles.excerpt: A checked or unchecked keyword is one of the few C# constructs that leaves no direct fingerprint in metadata. There is no attribute, no flag, no scope record that says "overflow checking was on here."…
articles.body: A checked or unchecked keyword is one of the few C# constructs that leaves no direct fingerprint in metadata. There is no attribute, no flag, no scope record that says "overflow checking was on here." The information survives in a completely different form: it is smeared across the individual arithmetic instructions, each of which comes in a checking and a non-checking variant. Reconstructing the keyword means reading those instructions back and working out the smallest block of source that would have produced exactly that pattern — and getting it wrong changes what the program does. This post walks the lowering in both directions and shows what Glass.NET rebuilds.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.

articles.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
articles.excerpt: SpaceX just made spaceflight history, catching the upper stage of its Starship megarocket when it returned to Earth. But Starship still has some pretty big boxes left to check.
articles.body: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running. The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. SpaceX wanted to bring both Starship elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But Ship came home successfully , nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.
